index.description: L2 index of tool packs. A tool is a real, dependency-free script an agent runs instead of writing a throwaway one. The retriever reads this to find an existing tool before writing code, then reads that tool's card — the card is the full contract, never the script. One meta.json per pack gates its scripts and cards. Authoring rules: tools/AGENTS.md.

pack.summary: Browser visual-regression tool pack, deliberately holding the two halves of the job that are stdlib and deterministic — it never drives a browser, because Playwright needs pip plus a ~150 MB download and a screenshot is non-deterministic by default. playwright-scaffold.py emits a determinism-hardened Playwright harness into the caller's own repo (fixed viewport per breakpoint, deviceScaleFactor 1, reduced motion, UTC, en-US, pinned colour scheme, frozen clock, font-hinting off, animation-kill CSS, networkidle plus an explicit settle assertion, and with --ci github a workflow pinning the Playwright container image, the only way font rasterisation stays stable across runners), refusing to overwrite without --force. png-diff.py compares two PNGs with a hand-rolled zlib+struct codec and fails on either of two gates: changed-pixel ratio, which catches drift, and largest 4-connected cluster, which catches a small structural shift that a ratio hides — and it refuses 16-bit, palette and interlaced input rather than guessing a green verdict over pixels it never read.

Cloudflare tool pack, built for output compression rather than API access: an MCP server hands the model the vendor's raw JSON and the model pays for every byte, so these three call the API and print only what changes a decision. zone-audit.py fans out over the per-setting endpoints (the batch settings endpoint is deprecated) and prints only the settings that violate a policy file, exiting 1 on a violation. dns-snapshot.py writes a canonically ordered JSONL snapshot of every DNS record and diffs it against a committed baseline, exiting 1 on drift and printing only the changed names. cache-purge.py chunks a purge to 100 operations per request, honours the 5-requests-per-minute plan limit, backs off on 429, is dry-run until --yes, and demands the zone name repeated as the value of --yes before it will purge everything.

Deploy safety tool pack, stdlib only and deliberately free: gating this makes free-tier output worse, and the tool that stops someone wiping their own .env is the tool that earns the upgrade. unit-lint.py reads a systemd unit against the filesystem it will run on and reports only what stops it starting — an ExecStart the deploy never rsynced or left non-executable, a WorkingDirectory that does not exist or that ProtectHome hides, an EnvironmentFile that is world-readable, a ReadWritePaths that does not cover where the app actually writes under ProtectSystem, a missing Restart or a 100ms RestartSec that burns the start limit, a relative path where systemd demands absolute, a Type=notify over a shell or interpreter that hangs 90 seconds and then fails, and a unit name that would silently replace an installed one. It is the half systemd-analyze verify cannot see, and every finding it prints is a twenty-minute edit-rsync-daemon-reload-journalctl loop that did not happen. smoke-check.py asserts what a deployed site actually serves rather than that something answered: per check a status, contains, not_contains, content-type, max latency and a minimum body size, and it is not_contains plus min_bytes that catch the failures a curl gate cannot — an incremental build that left a stale route directory behind, and an SPA shell served where content should be. Neither tool mutates anything: unit-lint writes nothing, smoke-check issues GET and HEAD only, and neither imports subprocess, because the repo is the source and a tool that fixes a unit in place edits the runtime instead.

Environment-topology tool pack: what a deployment target actually holds, and what it must never hold. Both tools are offline — no network, no credential, no subprocess. wrangler-env-lint.py names every binding and var a named Wrangler environment silently loses: Cloudflare documents bindings and environment variables as non-inheritable, so vars, kv_namespaces, d1_databases, r2_buckets, durable_objects, queues, services and secrets do not reach [env.production] from the top level while routes and workers_dev do, and the failure surfaces only as an undefined in production at request time. It also reports an unset compatibility_date and a durable object class bound without a migration that creates it, parses JSONC with its own string-aware comment and trailing-comma stripper because the standard library has none, and reads wrangler.toml through tomllib. secret-leak-scan.py finds committed credentials in a worktree, its CI config and optionally its built output — Supabase sb_secret_ keys and legacy service_role JWTs, decoded to read the role claim rather than pattern-matched because the publishable half of the legacy pair is the same shape and is meant to ship, Cloudflare cfut_ tokens, private key blocks, high-entropy assignments and a real .env that .gitignore does not cover — and never prints a secret: a finding is file:line, the rule, the severity and at most the first 8 characters. It scans the worktree only, deliberately not git history.

Game backend tool pack: hmac-rng-golden.py (emit/verify golden vectors for HMAC-SHA256 rejection-sampling randomness, four counter/word variants) and deploy-scaffold.py (systemd unit + nginx vhost + deploy.sh with every collidable identity namespaced by --name, regex locations always quoted).

GitHub Actions supply-chain tool pack. gha-audit.py statically audits workflow YAML against 14 rules, each drawn from a real 2025-26 incident — a mutable action tag (tj-actions/changed-files, CVE-2025-30066, ~23k repos retagged), a pull-request title interpolated into run: (Nx s1ngularity, 2,180 accounts), pull_request_target checking out the fork's head, toJSON(secrets) or a secret beside curl (GhostAction, 3,325 secrets), missing permissions, permissions write-all, workflow-scope id-token, missing concurrency or timeout-minutes, ubuntu-22.04, persist-credentials left at its default, curl piped to sh — and prints only the offending line, its severity and the fix, failing at or above --fail-on. gha-pin.py resolves every uses: owner/repo@tag to the 40-char commit SHA through the GitHub API, rewrites it in place with the tag kept as a comment, and --check is the drift gate that keeps a repository pinned. Workflows are read by an indentation-aware mini-lexer, not a YAML parser, because a tool pack ships no dependencies.

Hetzner Cloud tool pack, built for output compression rather than API access: hcloud already wraps the API, so these two correlate across sources and print only what changes a decision. baseline-audit.py scores one box against a CIS-derived baseline by joining the account side (firewall attached, SSH open to the world, Cloud Backups paid for and the snapshot age) with box-side evidence the caller already gathered from sshd -T, ss -tulpnH and sysctl -a, never shelling out and never running a command on the host; it prints one line per failing item, treats unverifiable as unmet, prices the Backups surcharge, holds every auto-fix when no out-of-band escape is verified, and refuses the run outright when an expired waiver is still covering a failing item. fw-sync.py converges a cloud firewall from the same spec behind the guard that justifies the tool: set_rules is a destructive replace, so it proves inbound SSH survives for every admin CIDR and for the caller's own source before any write, exits 5 rather than locking anyone out, and arms a revert of the prior rule set that only a second invocation carrying --commit can cancel. Neither can delete a server, volume, snapshot or image; Hetzner Robot dedicated servers are out of scope.

Python web tool pack: venv-bootstrap.sh (idempotent .venv create + requirements install + import proof) and django-test-gate.py (run a Django suite through the project venv, emit one JSON verdict line, exit 0/1/2), each with an instruction card that is the full contract.

Research tool pack: source-table.py turns a JSONL of claims into a markdown evidence table plus a gaps report and exits 1 when any load-bearing claim carries no source, so an unsourced research arm fails loudly instead of shipping.

Issue-tracker pack built as one generic transport plus one methodology tool, deliberately not as a per-vendor client: every SaaS API breaks eventually and a shipped client that 500s on a customer's machine costs more trust than a missing feature. api-call.py is the only networking code — a declarative profile per vendor (base URL, auth header shape, pagination by page, cursor or Link header, named operations) and a --select path expression that shapes the response down to the fields the caller named, so a list of 40 issues costs 40 short rows instead of 40 vendor envelopes. That compression is the justification for duplicating something the vendors already ship: ClickUp's official MCP server is capped at 50 calls per 24 hours on Free against roughly 144,000 a day for the REST API, and every call it does answer bills the model for the whole envelope. It is dry-run until --yes, honours Retry-After on a 429, and exits 3 on an absent credential, 4 on a rejected one and 6 on a vendor error, so a calling agent can tell 'you have no credential' from 'I crashed'. sdd-sync.py reconciles a feature's SDD task files — the todo/, in-progress/, done/ directory-as-status lifecycle — against a tracker snapshot through a hash ledger that persists task file to remote id to last hash. The ledger is the point: without it a second run creates the whole task set again, every time, and it is also what lets the tool report local-ahead, remote-ahead and conflict rather than silently picking a winner. A conflict exits 1 and touches nothing; a plan the caller never executed is reported rather than recorded as synced. Ships profiles for GitHub Issues, Linear and ClickUp v2.

Static-site tool pack: asset-stamp.py appends each asset's own content hash to the URL the HTML emits, so a CDN edge holding an immutable copy is forced to fetch the new bytes while unchanged assets keep their URL and stay cached — and in --check mode it fails a build whose pages still point at a stale or unstamped asset. Derived from a measured incident where an edge served a three-day-old file with cf-cache-status HIT for hours after a green deploy, because nothing in the pipeline looks at what the edge actually serves.

Template assembly tool pack, stdlib only and deliberately free: it is mechanism, and gating the mechanism that makes an agent's output correct only makes free-tier output worse. tpl-build.py assembles one source template or an ordered block set into Markdown plus a self-contained HTML copy, resolving every declared parameter explicit value, then project store, then declared default, then ask — and a required parameter that reaches the end of that order with nothing to fill it is refused by name rather than substituted empty, which is the difference between a template that fails loudly and a document shipped with a hole in it. The template language is {{name}} substitution plus sections gated on `when: var in [literal, ...]` and nothing else: expressions, loops, filters, Mustache partials, dotted paths, YAML anchors, block scalars and every other construct are each refused by name, because the same assembler runs on behalf of other accounts and a general template language there is a server-side template injection surface. An assembly is blocks plus literal passthrough, because measured over the corpus blocks cover the envelope and the median template shares no bytes with any other: --use takes block references and .md file paths in one ordered list, and a section matching no block is assembled from literals rather than treated as an error. The Markdown to HTML renderer is partial on purpose and says so — headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, fenced code, blockquotes, links, emphasis — escaping everything else, and it runs two escaping paths that never meet: source text is escaped entity-preservingly, so the 58-file family that already stores <artefact_id> is not double-escaped into visible entities, while a substituted value is held as an opaque sentinel through the whole render and escaped unconditionally at the end, so it can neither open a tag nor forge a heading nor break out of a table cell, and only http, https, mailto and relative hrefs are ever resolved. A successful build then remembers what it was given: every --set or --values answer is written to the project store so the next build asks for less, while a value that came from a declared default is deliberately never persisted, because freezing a default means a later change to the block silently stops taking effect and nothing in the project explains why; --no-remember opts out. tpl-params.py is the ask channel: it lists every declared parameter with its type, requiredness, default and whether the project store already answers it, and emits as JSON exactly which parameters are unresolved and the question to ask for each, flagging a text parameter as prose an LLM composes rather than a value a user types. It manages the store at {project}/.faion/template-params.json and a sensitive parameter never reaches it: the store records that the parameter exists and its placeholder, never the value, and any value matching a known secret shape is refused whatever the declaration says. tpl-migrate.py is the third tool and the one that makes the other two reachable for the 1,670 templates carrying <Angle> placeholders and the 556 carrying [bracket] ones: it extracts every candidate placeholder with its position, its heading and the label beside it, proposes a snake_case name, a guessed type and a description drafted from that surrounding context rather than invented, and emits the declaration plus the rewritten body to stdout or a chosen path — the template itself is never touched without --write. What it refuses to do is the point: a placeholder is not automatically a parameter, so prose guidance to a reader, a bare FILL carrying no name, a choice list or date format with no label to name it, a placeholder inside a code fence or code span, an already-HTML-escaped <name> and two placeholders that normalise onto one name are each reported by reason and LEFT ALONE, because a declaration for something that was never a parameter makes tpl-build refuse a build by name forever after. Every rewrite is parsed back before it is written and dropped whole if it does not round-trip, and a template that already declares variables is refused a second block rather than merged. --report runs the same analysis over every template under a root and prints the migration surface — how many map cleanly, how many are prose, which proposed names recur across the corpus and are therefore the parameters worth standardising — which is the table that says whether migration is a week or a quarter.

Web reading tool pack, stdlib only: polite-fetch.py fills an on-disk cache with a ledger from a URL list and makes the politeness mechanical — robots.txt consulted per host before the first content request and treated as disallow when it cannot be read, a one-second floor between requests that no flag can lower, a truthful faion-web-parse User-Agent whose only variable part is the contact address, 200 requests and 120 s per host per run unless the host is one you assert you own, no cookie jar and no auth-wall circumvention, and a distinct exit code so a robots-truncated crawl can never be mistaken for a complete one. page-extract.py turns that cache into readable text or markdown plus JSON-LD, OpenGraph and microdata in one pass per page, writing JSONL to a file so raw HTML never reaches the model, and it fixes the bug that quietly breaks every hand-rolled html.parser scraper: HTMLParser fires no end tag for an implied one, so unclosed li and p elements corrupt the depth stack and mis-nest structured data on most real pages. Contact fields are never emitted and emails in prose are redacted.
